answers.primary: A PostToolUse hook in the project's .claude/settings.json with matcher "Edit|Write", narrowed with the handler-level "if": "Edit(**/*.ts)" field, running a command that reads .tool_input.file_path from the hook's stdin JSON and invokes the formatter on exactly that file. The hook replaces the startup instruction so the format step is executed by Claude Code rather than chosen by the model.
answers.rejected_alternative: Keeping the rule in CLAUDE.md or a .claude/rules file, which is the configuration already in place: it is advisory context that shapes intent but never guarantees the step, which is why it is skipped every few sessions.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude Code fires PostToolUse after every matching tool call regardless of whether the model remembered the convention, and the model has no say in whether the hook runs.
answers.context_boundary: The hook runs in its own OS process outside the model's context window; the CLI passes tool_input, tool_response and duration_ms in on stdin. Only what the hook returns (a decision, reason, or additionalContext) crosses back, so the reformatted bytes on disk are invisible to Claude until it re-reads the file.
answers.lifecycle: Fires after each successful Edit or Write whose path matches, in any session that loads that settings file, and reloads automatically when the file is edited. It stops applying if the hook block is removed, if disableAllHooks is set, or if a managed strictPluginOnlyCustomization or allowManagedHooksOnly policy blocks project-level hooks.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open. PostToolUse runs after the write has already landed and cannot undo it, and a formatter that exits non-zero (anything but 2) only prints a hook error notice while the unformatted edit stands. It also misses files Claude creates through Bash (heredoc, sed, codegen), so pair it with a Stop hook that formats everything git status --porcelain reports if the commit gate must be airtight.
answers.version_caveat: No version gate on the hook itself. The comma-separated matcher form "Edit,Write" needs Claude Code v2.1.191 or later, and the "if" filter is best-effort: it fails open and runs the hook anyway when the tool input cannot be parsed, so it must not be relied on as the only filter. The practical dependency is jq (or an equivalent JSON parser) existing on every developer machine.

answers.primary: permissions.deny rules committed in the repository's .claude/settings.json: Read(./.env), Read(./.env.*), Read(**/.env) and Read(./secrets/**), with matching Edit(...) deny entries for the same paths. Deny rules are evaluated before ask and allow, are not gated by the workspace trust dialog (only allow rules and additionalDirectories are), and cannot be re-opened by any user-level setting or CLI flag, so every teammate inherits them on clone.
answers.rejected_alternative: A PreToolUse hook that inspects tool_input.file_path and exits 2 on a match. It has the same subprocess blind spot, adds a script to maintain, and can be switched off with disableAllHooks, so it buys nothing over a deny rule here.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. Permission rules are enforced by Claude Code itself, not by the model; prompt or CLAUDE.md text shapes what Claude attempts but never changes what is allowed.
answers.context_boundary: Evaluated inside the CLI process before the tool executes, so nothing about the secret ever enters the model's context window; Claude only sees a denial message. A path-scoped rule leaves the Read tool available and blocks only the matching calls, unlike a bare-name deny which would strip the tool from Claude's context entirely.
answers.lifecycle: Applies from session start to every Read, Grep, Glob, @-file mention and IDE-shared selection, plus file-reading Bash commands Claude Code recognizes. It applies for as long as the file is present in the repo and can only be lifted by editing the committed file, which is a reviewable change.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed for the built-in file tools and for recognized Bash file commands such as cat, head, tail and sed, but fails open for arbitrary subprocesses: a Python or Node script that opens the path itself is not covered. The other common trap is path anchoring, where a single leading slash anchors at the settings source rather than the filesystem root, so a rule silently matches nothing.
answers.version_caveat: From v2.1.208 a Read deny rule also blocks the Edit tool on the same path, but Write and NotebookEdit are still not covered, so explicit Edit(...) deny rules are required. From v2.1.210 Claude Code warns at startup that path rules written for Write, NotebookEdit or Glob are accepted but never consulted. For enforcement that also stops spawned processes you need sandbox filesystem settings, which are macOS, Linux and WSL2 only.

answers.primary: A Notification hook in each engineer's ~/.claude/settings.json with matcher "permission_prompt" (add a second group with "idle_prompt" to also catch the waiting-for-your-next-prompt case), running the platform's native notifier: osascript on macOS, notify-send on Linux, or a PowerShell toast or MessageBox on Windows.
answers.rejected_alternative: A PermissionRequest hook. It fires at the right moment but its job is to answer the permission decision, and wiring notification logic into it risks a hook that accidentally allows or defers prompts instead of merely announcing them.
answers.enforcement_owner: Shared: the harness deterministically fires the Notification event and spawns the command, but the OS notification daemon owns actual delivery, so a fired hook is not a guaranteed alert.
answers.context_boundary: The hook command runs in a separate process with the notification payload on stdin; nothing enters or leaves the model's context window. The run stays blocked in the CLI waiting for the human either way.
answers.lifecycle: Fires each time Claude Code emits a notification of the matched type, for the life of every session on that machine, and stops at session end. The agent_needs_input and agent_completed matchers additionally only fire while agent view is open, so they are not a substitute for permission_prompt.
answers.failure_mode: Purely advisory and fails open: a missed alert never blocks or delays the run, it just leaves the session stalled longer. osascript fails silently unless Script Editor has been granted notification permission, notify-send needs a running notification daemon, and a session over SSH, in a container, or headless with -p has no desktop to notify at all.
answers.version_caveat: No version gate for the Notification event or the permission_prompt and idle_prompt matchers; agent_needs_input and agent_completed require Claude Code v2.1.198 or later. Because the notify command is platform-specific, this belongs in user settings rather than a shared repository settings file, or it will be a broken command on half the fleet.

answers.primary: Managed settings deployed by IT, setting permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode to "disable" (and permissions.disableAutoMode if auto-approval also counts as prompting switched off). Deliver it through a channel the developer cannot write: the macOS com.anthropic.claudecode managed preferences domain via MDM, the Windows HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\ClaudeCode registry key via Group Policy or Intune, or /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json and C:\Program Files\ClaudeCode\managed-settings.json.
answers.rejected_alternative: The same disableBypassPermissionsMode key in the developer's own ~/.claude/settings.json. It works technically (the key is honored from any scope) but the developer owns that file and can delete the line, which is exactly the loophole being closed.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. Managed settings sit at the top of the precedence chain, above command line arguments and above every user, project and local settings file, so --dangerously-skip-permissions and --permission-mode bypassPermissions are refused at startup.
answers.context_boundary: Read by the CLI process at startup, entirely outside any context window. Nothing about the policy reaches the model except the practical consequence that permission prompts keep appearing during its tool calls.
answers.lifecycle: Applies from process start for every session on the enrolled device and re-applies on the settings reload when the policy file changes. It stops applying only when the device leaves management or the policy is removed; there is a bypass_permissions_disabled SessionEnd reason for sessions terminated because the mode was revoked mid-flight.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed on a managed device, but the boundary is the machine and not the person: an unenrolled laptop, a container image, a cloud VM, or a WSL distro without wslInheritsWindowsSettings simply has no policy file and no restriction. On Windows the HKCU policy hive is user-writable and is consulted only when no admin-level source exists, so the HKLM key must actually be deployed or a developer can supply their own policy.
answers.version_caveat: No minimum version for the key itself, but the legacy Windows path C:\ProgramData\ClaudeCode\managed-settings.json stopped being read at v2.1.75 and must be migrated to C:\Program Files\ClaudeCode\. Pair it with disableSideloadFlags (v2.1.193 or later) so a single run cannot sideload configuration, and with forceRemoteSettingsRefresh if the policy is delivered by server-managed settings and you need startup to fail closed when the fetch fails.

answers.primary: A Stop hook. The deterministic shape is a pair: a PostToolUse hook on Bash writes a pass marker (session id, turn boundary, timestamp, exit status) when the test command succeeds, and a command-type Stop hook checks for a marker belonging to the turn that is ending and returns {"decision": "block", "reason": "..."} when it is absent, which sends the reason back as Claude's next instruction. Where the check must inspect real state rather than a marker, use an agent-type Stop hook that runs the suite itself.
answers.rejected_alternative: A CLAUDE.md or rules instruction saying to always run tests before declaring work complete. That is the exact instruction the model forgets, so restating it more emphatically does not change the enforcement class.
answers.enforcement_owner: Split by design: the harness fires Stop and enforces the block, but the model owns the remediation because only it can go run the tests and fix what fails. The hook can refuse the ending, not produce a passing suite.
answers.context_boundary: The hook runs out-of-process and receives stop_hook_active, last_assistant_message, background_tasks and transcript_path on stdin. Only the reason or additionalContext string crosses back into the same session's context window, where it becomes the model's next instruction. An agent-type hook runs its verification in a separate subagent context and returns only ok plus reason.
answers.lifecycle: Fires every time the main agent finishes responding, which is not the same as task completion, so it fires on conversational turns too. It does not fire on a user interrupt, and API errors route to StopFailure instead. The marker must be scoped to the current turn or the hook goes stale and passes a turn that ran tests an hour earlier.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed at first and then degrades to fail open: Claude Code overrides the hook and ends the turn after 8 consecutive blocks, so a hook that never converges eventually lets the unverified turn through. A hook that ignores stop_hook_active will hit that cap on every run. A marker-file design is also gameable in the weak sense that the model can satisfy it by running a trivially narrow subset of tests.
answers.version_caveat: No version gate on command-type Stop hooks. Agent-type hooks are explicitly experimental and may change, with a 60 second default timeout and a 50 tool-turn ceiling; prompt-type hooks default to 30 seconds and judge only from the hook input. CLAUDE_CODE_STOP_HOOK_BLOCK_CAP raises the 8-block cap, and /goal is the built-in session-scoped shortcut for a prompt-based Stop hook if you want the behavior without config.

answers.primary: An explicit ask rule in settings: "ask": ["Bash(git push *)"], placed in managed settings (or at minimum the committed project settings) so it cannot be edited away, plus PowerShell(git push *) on Windows fleets. Content-scoped ask rules are the documented exception that still forces a prompt under bypassPermissions and auto mode, and they survive a sandbox's autoAllowBashIfSandboxed substitution.
answers.rejected_alternative: A PreToolUse hook returning permissionDecision "ask". It does fire in every permission mode and would work, but it is one more script that disableAllHooks or a hook-loading policy can suppress, whereas the ask rule's precedence is guaranteed by the permission engine.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. Permission rules are evaluated by Claude Code before the tool runs; the model cannot approve its own push, and no permission mode the session was launched with removes an explicit ask rule.
answers.context_boundary: Evaluated in the CLI process before execution. The confirmation happens in the terminal UI, entirely outside the context window; the model sees only the approved-or-denied outcome as its tool result.
answers.lifecycle: Checked on every matching Bash call for the whole session. An ask rule never persists an approval, so it prompts each time rather than once per repository. It stops applying only if the rule is removed from the settings source that supplies it.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed for the literal pattern but is fragile at the edges, because Bash argument matching is string matching: git -C dir push, an aliased or wrapper-invoked push, devbox run git push, or a push buried inside a shell script the model executes will not match Bash(git push *). Two mode caveats also change the outcome rather than the safety: dontAsk mode denies instead of prompting, and a headless -p run has no human to answer so the call is refused.
answers.version_caveat: No version gate on ask rules. Note the interaction documented for sandboxing: when the sandbox is enabled with autoAllowBashIfSandboxed left at true, a bare Bash ask rule is substituted away by the sandbox boundary, but a content-scoped rule like Bash(git push *) still forces the prompt, which is why the rule must be written with the specifier rather than as a whole-tool ask.

answers.primary: A PostToolUse hook with matcher "Bash" (and "PowerShell" on Windows) that appends tool_input.command together with session_id, cwd, timestamp and the tool_response exit status to an append-only record, or a type: "http" hook that POSTs the same payload to a central collector. Deploy it through managed settings so it is present on every developer machine rather than opt-in.
answers.rejected_alternative: A PreToolUse logging hook. It fires earlier and catches more, but it records attempted calls including ones that were then denied or never executed, which is the wrong evidentiary record when the requirement is what actually ran.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. The hook fires on the CLI's own dispatch path whether or not the model cooperates or even mentions the command, which is precisely why it beats self-reporting.
answers.context_boundary: Runs in a separate process (or a remote endpoint for the HTTP form) and receives tool_input, tool_response and duration_ms from the CLI. Nothing needs to cross back into the model's context: the hook exits 0 with no stdout, so the audit trail is invisible to the session it is auditing.
answers.lifecycle: Fires after every successful tool call matching the matcher, for as long as the settings source that defines it is loaded. Add a PostToolUseFailure hook with the same matcher to also capture commands that started and then errored, otherwise failed executions leave no record.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open as a control: it records what Claude Code dispatched, not what the shell ultimately did, so a single command that invokes a script, bash -c, a Makefile target or a background job hides the real work behind one log line. A local log file is also writable by the very developer being audited, and a hook that crashes does not stop the command. Ship to a remote collector and lock the hook down if the record has to hold up.
answers.version_caveat: allowManagedHooksOnly is managed-settings-only and is what stops a developer's own settings from replacing or shadowing the audit hook; note also that disableAllHooks in a user settings file does not disable managed hooks unless it is set in managed settings too. HTTP hook destinations can be pinned with allowedHttpHookUrls and their env interpolation with httpHookAllowedEnvVars. On Windows set "shell": "powershell" on the hook command.

answers.primary: A PreToolUse hook on Bash that parses tool_input.command and returns permissionDecision "deny" for every aws invocation that is not the approved read-only form, combined with an allow rule Bash(aws s3 ls) (plus Bash(aws s3 ls *) if arguments are wanted) so the approved call runs with no prompt. Narrow the hook with "if": "Bash(aws *)" so the process only spawns for aws commands.
answers.rejected_alternative: A deny rule Bash(aws *) paired with an allow rule Bash(aws s3 ls). The docs are explicit that deny is evaluated first and rule specificity does not change the order, so the broad deny would block the approved call as well: a deny rule cannot carry allowlist exceptions.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness on both halves. The hook decision and the allow rule are both evaluated by Claude Code before the command executes, and PreToolUse fires ahead of the permission-mode check in every mode, including bypassPermissions and dontAsk.
answers.context_boundary: The hook runs in its own process with only the command string handed to it; the deny reason string is the sole thing that crosses back into the model's context, where it becomes the tool error the model reads and adjusts to.
answers.lifecycle: Runs before every Bash tool call for the whole session and reloads with the settings file. It applies to any session that loads the hook, so deploy it in managed settings if the shutoff must hold on machines whose owners would rather it did not.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed only if the script is written default-deny and exits 2 on its own internal errors; any other non-zero exit is treated as a hook error and the command proceeds, which is a fail-open path a naive script walks straight into. Command-string matching is the real weakness: compound commands, leading env assignments, wrapper runners, bash -c, a profile flag before the subcommand, or a Python boto3 script all evade it, and the allow rule's word boundary means aws s3 ls matches while a double-spaced variant does not.
answers.version_caveat: No version gate on PreToolUse deny decisions or on Bash allow rules. The "if" filter is best-effort and fails open by running the hook when a command cannot be parsed, which is the safe direction here since the hook is the deny side. If the aws surface has to be genuinely closed rather than pattern-matched, move the boundary to credentials and network (sandbox credentials.envVars deny on AWS variables, or IAM) rather than to string matching.

answers.primary: Enable sandboxing: sandbox.enabled true with sandbox.filesystem.denyRead listing ~/.aws/credentials and ~/.ssh, or the equivalent sandbox.credentials.files entries with mode "deny". This is OS-level isolation (Seatbelt on macOS, bubblewrap plus seccomp on Linux and WSL2) that applies to the Bash tool and every process descended from it, which is exactly the layer path-based permission rules do not reach.
answers.rejected_alternative: More Read(...) deny rules, or a PreToolUse hook that scans Bash commands for those paths. Both operate on what Claude Code itself can see and inspect, and neither can stop a Python interpreter that has already been launched from calling open() on the file.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness sets the boundary and the OS kernel enforces it. Once the sandbox is up, nothing the model decides and nothing a spawned process does can reopen the path.
answers.context_boundary: Enforcement happens at the process boundary of the sandboxed Bash command, outside every context window. What reaches the model's context is only the resulting permission-denied error in the command's stderr, which it can read and react to but not route around.
answers.lifecycle: Applies to each sandboxed Bash invocation from session start onward. Commands listed in sandbox.excludedCommands and calls that pass dangerouslyDisableSandbox run outside the boundary, so set allowUnsandboxedCommands to false to close that escape hatch, and keep excludedCommands minimal.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open by default in the one case that matters most: if the sandbox cannot start because bwrap or socat is missing or the platform is unsupported, Claude Code prints a warning and runs commands unsandboxed. Set failIfUnavailable true to make it a hard startup gate. It also covers only Bash and its children, so the model's own in-process Read tool still needs the matching Read deny rule; the two sets are merged into the final boundary.
answers.version_caveat: Sandboxing is macOS, Linux and WSL2 only, so a native Windows fleet gets no coverage from this mechanism at all. sandbox.credentials.files and credentials.envVars require v2.1.187 or later, filesystem.disabled requires v2.1.216, network.strictAllowlist requires v2.1.219, and filesystem.allowManagedReadPathsOnly is managed-settings-only (it locks allowRead to managed entries while denyRead still merges from every source).

answers.primary: Managed settings with strictPluginOnlyCustomization set to true, which locks all four named surfaces at once: hooks (the automation scripts), skills (the on-demand instruction packages), agents (the custom agent definitions) and mcp (the external tool servers). Combine it with strictKnownMarketplaces to pin where plugins may come from, enabledPlugins in the same managed source to force-enable the vetted plugins, and disableSideloadFlags to reject --plugin-dir, --plugin-url, --agents and --mcp-config.
answers.rejected_alternative: allowManagedHooksOnly together with allowManagedMcpServersOnly. Those two locks are real but cover only hooks and MCP servers, leaving ~/.claude/skills, .claude/skills, ~/.claude/agents and .claude/agents loading normally, which is half the stated requirement.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. For each locked surface the loader skips user-level and project-level sources entirely and loads only plugin-provided and managed-policy sources, and managed settings cannot be overridden by any other scope including command line arguments.
answers.context_boundary: This is a load-time decision inside the CLI process. Its effect on context is that a blocked skill, agent or MCP tool never appears to the model in the first place, so there is nothing to invoke and no instruction to ignore: the surface is absent rather than forbidden.
answers.lifecycle: Evaluated at startup and again on each settings reload, for every session on a managed device. Blocked marketplace sources are checked before any network request, so they never touch the filesystem, and the restriction re-applies on plugin install, update, refresh and auto-update. It stops applying if the device leaves management.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed on a managed device and fails open off it: an unenrolled machine, a container image, or an older CLI build has no policy to enforce. Two quieter gaps: unrecognized surface names in the array are ignored rather than rejected, so a typo silently leaves a surface unlocked, and CLAUDE.md, .claude/rules and slash commands are not among the four locked surfaces, so instruction-shaped customization still flows in from repos.
answers.version_caveat: strictPluginOnlyCustomization and strictKnownMarketplaces are managed-settings-only and have no effect in user or project settings; disableSideloadFlags requires Claude Code v2.1.193 or later. Managed settings parse tolerantly, so an entry that fails validation is stripped with a warning while the rest of the policy stays enforced, which means a broken lock can go unnoticed: validate with claude doctor on a test machine before a fleet rollout.
